items.title: 4-figure grid references give 1 km precision; 6-figure give 100 m
items.claim: What precision do OS grid references provide?

options.text: 4-figure references identify a 1 km × 1 km square; 6-figure references identify a 100 m × 100 m square; 8-figure references give 10 m precision — read 'eastings before northings', 'along the corridor, up the stairs'
References are accurate to 1 metre regardless

items.reveal:
OS uses a National Grid: read eastings (horizontal) first, then northings (vertical). Grid letters (NY, SE, etc.) identify 100 km squares.

A full reference combines letters with numerical eastings/northings — e.g. SE 543 367 for 100 m precision. The National Grid covers Great Britain; Northern Ireland uses the Irish Grid; the Channel Islands use UTM.

GPS coordinates (latitude/longitude or UTM) are international alternatives. Reporting accident or weather locations with inconsistent precision causes real navigation failures, including in search-and-rescue.
items.why: Map references are not arbitrary precision. Search and rescue, weather reporting and fieldwork all depend on consistent referencing — and the difference between 4 and 6 figures is the difference between 'somewhere in this 1 km square' and 'within a tennis court'.

items.title: Scotland is still rising — England is sinking
items.claim: What is happening to the British Isles vertically due to glacial isostatic adjustment?

options.text: Both are stable — Britain has fully recovered from the last Ice Age
Scotland and northern England rise by 1-2 mm/year as crust rebounds from glacial loading; southern and eastern England sink by around 1 mm/year
All of Britain is sinking equally
The British Isles tilt is not measurable

items.reveal:
When the last ice sheet melted (about 10,000 years ago), the depressed crust began to rise. The mantle's slow viscous flow means rebound is still happening. GPS networks (BIGF, the British Isles GNSS Facilities) measure the motion directly.

Net result for relative sea level: southern England experiences faster sea-level rise than would be expected from climate alone, while northern Scotland experiences slower (or even falling) relative sea level. This is one reason why Thames and Hull tidal defences face accelerating pressure.

Fenno-Scandinavia is rising even faster (10 mm/year in parts of the Gulf of Bothnia).
items.why: Climate-change sea-level projections must be combined with local geophysics. A coast is rising or sinking on its own terms, and the climate signal sits on top of that.

items.title: Meanders migrate downstream and laterally over time
items.claim: How do meanders change over time?

options.text: They are fixed channel features that do not change

Helical flow concentrates erosion on the outer bank (river cliff) and deposition on the inner bank (point bar); meanders migrate downstream and outward, eventually being cut off as oxbow lakes when meander necks are breached
Meanders only form in glacial rivers

items.reveal:
The thalweg (line of fastest flow) traces an S-curve through meanders, swinging from outer bank to outer bank. Bank erosion rates can be 1-10 m/year in alluvial rivers — Mississippi meander cutoffs were mapped by Harold Fisk in 1944 for the US Army Corps of Engineers, showing channel migration across tens of km of floodplain over centuries.

The Corps now actively manages cutoffs to prevent further channel shortening. The Carter Lake oxbow (Iowa/Nebraska) is on the Iowa side of the modern Missouri River because of a single cutoff in 1877.

Floodplain land is dynamic. Property built on meander-prone rivers faces migration as well as flood risk.
items.why: Floodplains are not static. Long-term planning has to account for channel movement, not just discharge — a slower hazard but no less inevitable.
